# What's under the hood

An explanatory piece for readers who know front-end frameworks and have read
Declare's homepage, the "Why" essay and the FAQ. Its premise: a Declare front
end is one complete artifact, and the runtime is what has to be true underneath
for that to hold. It follows one program from source to pixels: what the
compiler produces, what a click does, who decides where things are, where the
host begins, and how a Declare program meets code that isn't Declare.

The page is itself a Declare program, and its figures are live views rather
than pictures: morphs are sprung scalars, and the hit-testing figure reports
the runtime's own answers. Open it with `?render=canvas` and it is the same
page, drawn directly to pixels.

Sizes quoted here were measured 2026-09-18 from real `declarec` production
builds (gzip, default level).

include [ "../homepage/fonts.declare", "parts/kit.declare", "parts/hero.declare", "parts/compile.declare", "parts/ships.declare", "parts/click.declare", "parts/hit.declare" ]

// The page's palette, light and dark. A token record is the language's own
// notation for this, so the tokens are declarations rather than a JavaScript
// object a `{ }` body happens to hold — and the App spreads one over a library
// preset below, so the few library widgets on the page find every token they
// read. The five layer hues (app, lib, run, ker, host) are the page's code.

theme Paper [
    ground = #F4F6F7, panel = #FFFFFF, sunk = #EBEFF1, line = #D5DDE3,
    ink = #15202A, lead = #34434F, body = #2A3843, muted = #5B6B78, faint = #8796A2,
    codeBg = #E8EDF0,
    accent = #2F6BDE, accentHover = #1F55BD,
    app = #2F6BDE, appSoft = #E3ECFC,
    lib = #0F9488, libSoft = #DDF3EF,
    run = #CF7B22, runSoft = #FBEBD8, runSoft0 = #FDF5EB,
    ker = #C23A5C, kerSoft = #F8E1E7,
    host = #6B7788, hostLine = #9AA6B3, hostSoft = #EDF0F3
    ]


theme Ink [
    ground = #0E1418, panel = #151D23, sunk = #1A242B, line = #26333D,
    ink = #E6ECF0, lead = #BBC7D0, body = #C9D3DA, muted = #8E9DA9, faint = #66757F,
    codeBg = #1E2931,
    accent = #6E9CF5, accentHover = #93B6FA,
    app = #5F8FF0, appSoft = #17263F,
    lib = #2DB7A7, libSoft = #11302D,
    run = #E59A45, runSoft = #3A2A17, runSoft0 = #221C15,
    ker = #E3637F, kerSoft = #3A1C25,
    host = #8C98A8, hostLine = #5A6775, hostSoft = #1B242B
    ]


App [ appName = "What's under the hood · Declare",

    // hosted: when a page mounts this program in an AppIsland (the homepage's
    // Architecture view), the host provides its appearance and type (read
    // here with hostProvided), and the page lengthens instead of this app scrolling
    // itself — so the host's own page scroll carries the article. Standalone,
    // the defaults hold and the app follows the system.

    hosted: boolean = { hostProvided("hosted", false) },
    face: string = { hostProvided("face", "") },
    headWeight: number = { hostProvided("headWeight", 600) },
    inDark: boolean = { hostProvided("dark", app.dark) },
    headTrack: number = { app.headWeight >= 900 ? -0.006 : app.headWeight >= 700 ? -0.014 : -0.02 },

    // this app's full height, exposed for the host to size its island to
    // (the host reads it as `island.exposed("docH", 0)`)

    exposes = ["docH"],
    docH: number = { this.page.y + this.page.height },

    scrolls = { app.hosted ? "none" : "y" },
    theme = { app.inDark ? ({ ...SanFranciscoDark, ...Ink }) : ({ ...SanFrancisco, ...Paper }) },

    // hosted, the app paints no ground: the host's own paper shows through

    fill = { app.hosted ? null : provided("theme").ground },

    // Helvetica, as on the homepage — unless a host hands down another face

    uiFace: string[] = { app.face == "avenir" ? Faces.avenir : Faces.helvetica },
    fontFamily = { app.uiFace },
    fontSize = 17,
    textColor = { provided("theme").body },

    // the two measures every edge on the page derives from

    col: number = { Math.min(680, app.width - 40) },
    wide: number = { Math.min(1060, app.width - 32) },

    // Fig. 1's two states: the reader switches between them

    heroMode: string = "looks",
    heroActual: boolean = { app.heroMode == "is" },

    // SELECTION IS PROVIDED ONCE, here, for the whole article. `selectable` is
    // a provided value, so a container opts its subtree in and each text leaf
    // reads the nearest provision — the type classes in the kit say nothing
    // about it, and a rich-text flow is selectable by its nature regardless.
    // The controls inside the figures are unaffected: every `Control` provides
    // `selectable = false` for its own label, which is the language's rule that
    // anything you activate is not copy.

    // The air above and below the article is the column's own padding. A padded
    // view has an inside: every child is placed from it, and the automatic
    // height counts the trailing inset back in, so `docH` measures the whole
    // article.

    page: View [ width = { app.col }, x = center, padding = [72, 0, 72, 0], selectable = true,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 40 ],

        // ── the masthead ──────────────────────────────────────────────

        masthead: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 18 ],
            Eyebrow [ text = "Declare · runtime architecture" ],
            Title [ fontSize = { app.width < 700 ? 40 : 54 }, text = "What’s under the hood" ],
            Dek [ text = "A Declare front end is one self-contained artifact — small enough to hold in your head, strict enough for a machine to verify, rich enough for an ambitious application. This is what Declare’s runtime does to make that true." ]
            ],

        // ── the lede ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

        lede: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 22 ],
            Para [ html = "Declare asks you to believe something unusual about an application’s front end: that it’s complete. Everything the interface does is written in the one program — where each box goes, how a paragraph wraps, what a click landed on, how a view becomes the next one, how a list of a million rows scrolls on a phone. It can be written that way because the program states the <i>relationships</i> between its elements rather than the steps that maintain them — which is both easier to understand and substantially more compact. A machine can verify it whole. And because the compiler sees every relationship in advance, the runtime never has to discover anything while it runs — which is why it was possible to write its hot path once, in a few kilobytes of C." ],
            Para [ html = "A promise like that puts a demand on what runs underneath. If the browser decided the layout, the program wouldn’t be complete. If a click were routed by the DOM, the same interface drawn directly to pixels would route it differently. So the runtime makes those decisions itself, once — and then hands the browser everything it is genuinely best at: real text, native fields, the page’s own scroll, links that behave like links. Declare isn’t a native framework running in a browser tab; it’s a language for interfaces with the feel of good native software that are also good citizens of the web — crawlable, selectable, responsive, touch-native. That the same program also runs drawn directly to pixels, and in a Mac application with no browser in it, is the proof that it really is complete: nothing about it was ever decided somewhere else. Figure 1 is that division of labor, before and after." ]
            ],

        // ── Fig. 1 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

        fig1: Figure [
            Caption [ fig = "Fig. 1 — Two pictures of one program",
                text = "Left: the stack a web framework implies — your file, a framework, and a browser that decides layout, text, and what you touched. Right: what runs — the compiled program, the library (itself written in Declare), a runtime that owns every one of those decisions, a small C kernel beneath it, and a host on the far side of one interface that realizes the result. The same five colors mark the same layers throughout." ],
            top: View [
                Segmented [ x = center, width = 300, height = 32,
                    value = { app.heroActual ? "is" : "looks" },
                    choices = { [ ({ id: "looks", label: "What it looks like" }), ({ id: "is", label: "What it is" }) ] },
                    input(v: object) { app.heroMode = "" + v }
                    ]
                ],
            Plate [ pad = 0,
                stage: HeroStage [ k = 0,
                    Spring [ attribute = k, to = { app.heroActual ? 1 : 0 }, stiffness = 60, damping = 14 ]
                    ]
                ],
            keys: View [
                legend: View [ x = center,
                    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 16 ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").app }, label = "App" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").lib }, label = "Library" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").run }, label = "Runtime" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").ker }, label = "Kernel" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").hostLine }, label = "Host" ]
                    ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 01 · The compiler ────────────────────────────────────────

        compile: Section [ num = "01", head = "The compiler",
            Para [ html = "The compiler is where completeness is enforced. It parses the brackets into a tree, resolves every bare name to an explicit path, extracts the read set of every <code>{ }</code> body, and type-checks each one as TypeScript against the real interface of every component — so an attribute that doesn’t exist, or a relationship that reads something it can’t, is an error before anything runs. What it emits is not code that builds a UI. It is a description of one: the tree with its attributes, a graph of which value reads which, and — for every body that is plain arithmetic over numeric slots — bytecode for a small stack machine." ],
            Para [ html = "One line from the homepage’s bouncing-ball demo, as it appears in the compiled artifact:" ],
            Trace [ ],
            Para [ html = "That last line never runs as JavaScript. In the calendar about 600 bodies take this path; the rest compile to ordinary functions the runtime calls back when their inputs change. A framework learns what depends on what while it runs — by re-running a component, or from a list you keep by hand. Here it is read off the source once, and the runtime never has to discover anything." ],
            Para [ html = "Because the program is data, it can be questioned as data. The Inspector on any page here — ⌥⌘D — reads this same graph: click a value and it shows the body that produced it, every path that body read, and their live values. That is not a debugging layer added to the runtime. It is the compiler’s output, still present at run time, answering a query." ]
            ],

        // ── 02 · What a click does ───────────────────────────────────

        run: Section [ num = "02", head = "What a click does",
            Para [ html = "When a handler writes an attribute, nothing updates yet. The write is queued. When the handler returns, the runtime performs one update: it finds every value that read what changed, recomputes each exactly once, in dependency order, and only then tells the host what moved. Declare calls that update a <b>settle</b> — the graph, disturbed by a write, coming back to rest — and it is the whole of the update model. If you know React, it is the nearest thing to a commit, except that nothing was rendered to compare against: the graph already knows what depends on what. The whole trip takes about a millisecond." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 2 — What a click sets in motion",
                    text = "The meter is live; its button is a library Button. Raise the level, then step through what your click set in motion. Four lanes: host, runtime, your code, kernel. Steps 5 and 6 are the split the compiler arranged in advance — arithmetic runs in the kernel; a template string is not arithmetic, so the kernel calls back into your compiled TypeScript, inside the same settle." ],
                ClickFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Steps 2 and 3 are the ones a web framework leaves to the browser: which element is under the pointer, and whether this was a click or the start of a drag. Here the runtime answers both, so hover, press, click-versus-drag and gesture ownership are one implementation — the same under a finger as under a pointer, and the same on every renderer." ],
            Para [ html = "Step 5 runs no JavaScript at all. Beneath the runtime sits a kernel: one C file, about 940 lines, that holds the graph’s tables — every attribute, every edge, the settle’s order — and evaluates the arithmetic the compiler turned into bytecode. In the browser it ships as WebAssembly, 11 KB gzipped inside the bundle; on the Mac the same source is linked in natively. It is unusual for a web framework to carry a C library, and it is only possible because the compiler left nothing for the runtime to work out: with every dependency and every arithmetic body known in advance, the bookkeeping of a settle is a fixed procedure over fixed tables, which is what C is for. A frame that only moves geometry — most animation frames — finishes inside it without entering JavaScript." ]
            ],

        // ── 03 · Motion ──────────────────────────────────────────────

        motion: Section [ num = "03", head = "Motion",
            Para [ html = "Continuity — a view becoming the next one rather than being replaced by it — is the part of good native software that is usually bespoke. Here is what makes it ordinary at run time. A <code>Spring</code> is an attribute with a target; each frame it writes its next value, and that write is a settle like any other — the same graph, the same kernel, the same dependency order. Nothing about animation is special-cased. Because geometry arithmetic runs as bytecode, a frame that only moves things — most frames of most animations — completes inside the kernel, in WebAssembly, and never enters JavaScript. Because a settle is one indivisible step, a new target arriving mid-flight is simply the next write: the spring retargets from wherever it is, and every value that read it follows. Interruptibility isn’t a feature of the animation system; it is what a reactive graph does when you write to it. And a layout is re-derived in the same settle, so an arrangement can travel as one thing — the calendar’s four views are one surface under a moving rectangle, and each frame of that zoom is a settle over the same few hundred kernel bodies." ]
            ],

        // ── 04 · Layout and hit-testing ──────────────────────────────

        geometry: Section [ num = "04", head = "Layout and hit-testing",
            Para [ html = "Open a Declare page in the browser’s element inspector and every view is there — a <code>div</code> per component, nested to mirror the tree — with its position and size written on it as inline style and no layout CSS anywhere. That is not a shortcut. It is the division of labor: every box is decided before the host hears about it, by one of three things. Arithmetic over slots (<code>x = { parent.width - 40 }</code>) runs in the kernel. A layout is a library class with one method, <code>place()</code>, returning a box per child — 1.8 KB of runtime applies it. An unset width is the bounding box of the visible children, kept current as a rule over the geometry table. Text is the one place the host contributes a number: it measures glyph widths. Wrapping, line count and the resulting height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer." ],
            Para [ html = "Because the runtime placed every box, it can answer the inverse question — what is under this point? — and that answer decides hover, press, whether a gesture was a click, and where a drag lands. The scene below computes none of it. Each view is reporting its own <code>hovered</code> fact, kept true by the same walk that routes a press." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 3 — Ask the runtime what is under the pointer",
                    text = "Try the rotated card’s corners, the empty-looking glass, the badge, and the child where the pane’s clip cuts it off. The walk runs in reverse paint order and stops at the first view that has declared an interest in the pointer." ],
                HitFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Drawn to pixels, or on the Mac, there is no DOM to ask, so this walk is the whole of hit-testing: clips subtracted, transforms inverted, scrollers corrected. In the DOM the browser names the element and the runtime resolves it to the nearest view with a handler. Either way the decision is one implementation, and the same one that decides whether a touch is a tap, a scroll, or a drag the page should not claim. Your program can ask it directly — <code>app.viewAt(x, y)</code> — which is how drag and drop is written." ]
            ],

        // ── 05 · Where the host begins ───────────────────────────────

        hosts: Section [ num = "05", head = "Where the host begins",
            Para [ html = "Everything above happens on one side of a single interface. It is called <code>Surface</code>, it has 58 methods — <code>setX</code>, <code>setFill</code>, <code>setText</code>, <code>setDrawing</code> — the runtime calls them and a backend implements them, and a view never learns which backend it has. Below that interface a backend does one job: realize what it was told. The DOM backend keeps a <code>div</code> per view with its geometry as inline style, and hands the platform what the platform does best — real text that selects and finds, the page’s own scroll, links that ⌘-click, native form fields. The canvas backend draws the whole tree directly to pixels, with its own compositor and its own scroll physics, for surfaces that must be uniform or capturable. The Mac host is a Swift application with no web engine in it: it runs the same runtime bundle in JavaScriptCore, links the same kernel as C, and applies one batch of drawing operations per settle to a tree of Core Animation layers." ],
            f4: Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 4 — One program, three hosts",
                    text = "The calendar’s build, drawn to scale by gzipped bytes. Switch hosts and watch what moves: the program, the library and the rest of the runtime are the same bytes; one block is exchanged, and on the Mac the kernel leaves the bundle for the executable. Beneath, the same desktop program with the same four windows open, on each host." ],
                sf: ShipsFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Drawing crosses the interface the same way. A view that needs a mark attributes can’t express — a gauge, a sparkline, an icon — defines <code>draw(d)</code>. It looks like canvas code but it records; the recording is plain data that the DOM backend rasterizes into the view’s own element, the canvas backend replays during its composite, and the Mac replays through Core Graphics. A drawing that read nothing that changed costs nothing." ],
            Para [ html = "Declare’s own model is single-threaded by construction: a settle is one step, and there is nothing in the language that runs concurrently with it. That is what lets hosts thread freely on their side of <code>Surface</code> — the canvas backend rasterizes drawings in a worker, and the Mac runs the runtime on a thread of its own and commits to the display on another. Your program never sees any of it." ]
            ],

        // ── 06 · Islands ─────────────────────────────────────────────

        islands: Section [ num = "06", head = "Interoperability",
            Para [ html = "<code>Surface</code> is the boundary between the runtime and its host. There is a second boundary, between a Declare program and code that isn’t Declare, and it has the same shape in every direction. A page embeds a Declare app by marking a sized element as its host — one attribute, <code>data-declare-embed</code> — and the app runs in that box like any other element on the page. The interface between them is declared, not improvised: the page <i>provides</i> values the app reads with <code>hostProvided</code>, the app <i>exposes</i> values the page reads back, and either side can <code>post</code> a message the other receives in <code>onPost</code>. Inside a Declare program the same contract runs the other way. A <code>DOMIsland</code> is a box the tree sizes and positions, inside which a video player, an editor or a React widget owns its own DOM. An <code>AppIsland</code> hosts a second Declare program as a tenant with the same provides, exposes and post — this article is one, mounted inside the homepage, taking its theme and type from the page around it. Three directions, one boundary, one vocabulary." ]
            ],

        // ── 07 · Why it still reads like a web page ──────────────────

        why: Section [ num = "07", head = "What remains the browser’s",
            Para [ html = "A Declare app in a browser is a web page, not an imitation of one. The behaviors that make a page a page stay the browser’s, and Declare does not simulate them: text is real text — it selects, it finds, it copies; fields are native fields, with native carets and input methods; scroll and overscroll are the page’s own; links are links, ⌘-click and all, and the Back button tells the truth; a crawler reads a static extraction from a plain host. The DOM renderer is the default because nothing about the program’s meaning is at stake in the browser, so all of that can be left to the browser without risk. A reader would struggle to tell a Declare page from any other." ],
            Para [ html = "What keeps that description honest is the second rendering. A program that owns its own semantics — no stylesheet, no browser layout engine to defer to — can be checked against another realization of itself, and the platform’s test suite holds the DOM renderer and the pixel renderer to the same picture on every change. The discipline that makes a front end complete is the same one that makes it mean exactly one thing." ],
            links: View [ width = 100%,
                layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 22, rowSpacing = 10 ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?render=canvas",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHover : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Reopen this page on the canvas renderer →" ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?viewer=reader",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHover : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Read this page’s source →" ]
                ]
            ],

        colophon: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],

            // nothing here claims a width — a y-axis stack never does — so the
            // rule derives its own from the parent's content box

            Divider [ ],
            Small [ width = 100%,
                text = "This page is a Declare program; every figure on it is made of views. Sizes were measured on 18 September 2026 from declarec production builds, gzipped at the default level." ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
